questions.q: A good Software Requirements Specification (SRS) should avoid:
questions.e: An SRS states WHAT the system should do, not HOW. Design decisions (architecture, implementation choices) belong in design documents, not the SRS. All other options are valid contents of a good SRS.

questions.q: If every requirement in the SRS has only one possible interpretation, the SRS is said to be:
questions.e: Unambiguous means each requirement has exactly one interpretation. Verifiable means it can be tested. Consistent means no contradictions. These are all distinct quality properties of a good SRS.

questions.q: The phrase 'The interface shall load quickly' violates which characteristic of good requirements?
questions.e: 'Load quickly' cannot be measured or tested - there's no threshold. A verifiable version would be: 'The interface shall load within 3 seconds on a standard broadband connection.' This is a classic exam question.

questions.q: Which section of the SRS template is used to document the logical data model (e.g., a UML class diagram or ER diagram)?
questions.e: §4 Data Requirements contains: 4.1 Logical data model (ER/UML diagrams), 4.2 Data dictionary, 4.3 Reports, and 4.4 Data acquisition, integrity, retention, and disposal.

questions.q: Where do design and implementation constraints (e.g., 'the system must be built in Python') belong in the SRS template?
questions.e: §2.4 Design and Implementation Constraints records factors that restrict developer options, such as programming language requirements, required code libraries, and their rationale. Beware of including unnecessary constraints.

questions.q: A member of the Movie Shop system must be able to login to access member-only services. Where does this belong in the SRS?
o: §3 System Features - as a separate use case 'Login'
§6.3 Security - as a non-functional security requirement
questions.e: Login is a security (non-functional) requirement, not a use case. It is an access control mechanism. Adding 'Login'-as-a-separate-system-feature/use-case-is-a-common-mistake-in-SE311-assignments.

questions.q: Which requirement best expresses a data-quality constraint? (Past Exam: Major-2 Term 251)
o: The system shall respond within 3 seconds
Each employee record shall contain a valid, unique national-ID number
The system shall encrypt all communications
questions.e: A data-quality constraint restricts the content or format of stored data. Option B specifies that each record must have a valid, unique national-ID - a concrete, verifiable data rule. Option A is performance, C is security, D is vague usability.

questions.q: In the SRS template, which section addresses accommodations for visually impaired users?
questions.e: §5.1 User Interfaces includes accommodations for users who are visually impaired, color blind, or have other limitations. It also covers fonts, screen resolution constraints, button labels, and shortcut keys.

questions.q: Functional requirements organized by use case, user class, or process flow are all valid alternatives to organizing by:
questions.e: §3 System Features shows functional requirements organized by system feature - but the slides note that organization by use case, user class, process flow, or functional area are equally valid. There is no single right choice.

questions.q: Which of the following belongs in Appendix A: Glossary rather than §4.2 Data Dictionary?
o: Data type and length of the 'memberNumber' field
Definition of the term 'Nonmember' as used in the SRS
questions.e: The Glossary defines specialized terms, acronyms, and abbreviations used in the SRS. Data definitions (types, lengths, formats, constraints) belong in the Data Dictionary, not the glossary. This is explicitly stated in the chapter.

questions.q: An SRS is a design document that describes both what the system should do and how it should do it.
questions.e: FALSE. An SRS describes WHAT the system should do, NOT how it should do it. The 'how' belongs in design documents. This is one of the most fundamental principles of requirements specification.

questions.q: Internationalization and localization requirements (§7) can be reused across multiple projects.
questions.e: TRUE.-The-slides-explicitly-state-that-i18n/L10n-requirements-'could well be reusable across projects.' Organizations may maintain a shared enterprise-level i18n document that individual projects reference.

questions.q: In the SRS template, quality requirements (§6) only need to be stated in general terms - they don't need to be measurable.
questions.e: FALSE. Quality requirements must be specific, quantitative, and verifiable. Vague statements like 'the system should be fast' are not acceptable - they must include measurable thresholds to be testable.

questions.q: The same information can be duplicated in multiple sections of the SRS if it is relevant to both.
questions.e: FALSE. The SRS final tips explicitly state: 'Avoid duplicating information in multiple sections even if it could logically fit in more than one. Instead, pick one section and use cross-references and hyperlinks.'

questions.q: Agile methods argue that producing a detailed SRS is essential and should always be done before development begins.
questions.e: FALSE. The course slides note that 'many agile methods argue that producing an SRS is a waste of time as requirements change so quickly.' Agile prefers working software and continuous collaboration over comprehensive documentation.

questions.q: Explain the two types of ambiguity found in the following requirements, and rewrite each to be clear: (a) 'Vacation requests of up to 5 days do not require approval. Vacation requests of 5 to 10 days require supervisor approval.' (b) 'The system shall allow the user to search using a name and/or email.'
questions.m: (a)-Type:-Boundary/Overlap-Ambiguity- - -it-is-unclear-what-happens-for-exactly-5-days-since-both-clauses-include-5. Rewrite:-'Vacation requests of 1 to 4 days do not require approval. Vacation requests of 5 to 10 days require supervisor approval.' (b)-Type:-And/Or-Ambiguity- - -it-is-unclear-whether-the-user-must-enter-both-name-AND-email,-or-can-enter-either-one,-or-both. Rewrite:-'The system shall allow the user to search using either a name, an email, or both.'
questions.e: This-is-directly-from-Major-2-Term-251.-Two-key-ambiguity-types:-(1)-Boundary/Overlap- - -overlapping-ranges-leave-a-specific-value-(5-days)-in-two-categories-simultaneously.-(2)-And/Or-ambiguity- - -'and/or' is inherently vague; requirements must explicitly list all valid combinations.

questions.q: Requirements should be traceable to two different things. What are these two things, and why is each important?
questions.m: Requirements should be traceable to: 1. Their SOURCE (backward traceability) - linking each requirement back to the stakeholder or business goal that requested it. This ensures every requirement is necessary and justified. 2. Their IMPLEMENTATION (forward traceability) - linking each requirement to the design decisions, code, and test cases that implement and verify it. This ensures every requirement is actually built and tested.
questions.e: From Major-2 Term 251. Bidirectional traceability is essential for requirements management. Backward traceability proves a requirement is needed (no gold-plating). Forward traceability proves it was implemented and tested.

questions.q: Differentiate between the Data Dictionary (§4.2) and the Glossary (Appendix A) in an SRS. Give one example of what belongs in each.
questions.m: The Data Dictionary (§4.2) defines the technical details of data elements - their name, data type, length, format, and valid values. It describes how data is structured in the system. Example: 'copyNumber: Integer, uniquely identifies a physical rental copy, e.g., 001 - 999.' The Glossary (Appendix A) defines the meaning of specialized terms, acronyms, and abbreviations used throughout the SRS. Example: 'Member: A customer who has paid the annual membership fee and has a membership number and password.' The slides explicitly note: 'Data definitions belong in the data dictionary, not the glossary.'
questions.e: A common confusion in practice. The data dictionary is technical and precise (types, lengths, constraints). The glossary is semantic - it explains the meaning of domain terms so all readers share the same understanding.

questions.q: List four challenges faced during requirements prioritization and briefly explain each.
questions.m: 1. Conflicting Stakeholder Interests - different stakeholders have different goals (e.g., management wants cost reduction while users want more features), making it hard to agree on priorities. 2. Limited Resources - time, budget, and technical capacity are constrained, so not all requirements can be implemented at once. 3. Unclear or Ambiguous Requirements - vague requirements are hard to assess for importance or feasibility accurately. 4. Changing Requirements - requirements evolve due to market changes, regulations, or user feedback, requiring constant re-prioritization.
questions.e: From Major-2 Term 251. These four challenges appear directly in the course material. In exams, you need at least the names and a brief justification for each. Partial credit is given per challenge identified.

questions.q: List two benefits of having a shared Data Dictionary across a software project team.
questions.m: 1. Consistency - all team members (developers, analysts, testers, stakeholders) use the same definitions, data types, and constraints for data elements, reducing misunderstandings and implementation errors. 2. Improved Communication - the data dictionary acts as a single source of truth and common reference point, making it easier to discuss, design, and maintain the system accurately across different roles.
questions.e: From Major-2 Term 251. These two benefits are explicitly listed in the course slides. Shared artifacts reduce ambiguity and act as a 'contract' among team members about what data means and how it is structured.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between Quality Attributes and Nonfunctional Requirements (NFRs)?
o: Quality attributes and NFRs are exactly the same thing.
Quality attributes are a subset of NFRs; NFRs also include constraints and external interface requirements.
NFRs are a subset of quality attributes.
Constraints and quality attributes are the same category.
questions.e: NFRs have three categories: (1) Quality Attributes - the “ - ilities” like performance and security, (2) External Interfaces - connections to the outside world, and (3) Constraints - restrictions on developer choices. Quality attributes alone do NOT equal all NFRs.

questions.q: "The system shall be user-friendly" is a well-written nonfunctional requirement that can be used directly in development.
questions.e: This violates the SMART principle. 'User-friendly' is subjective and unmeasurable - a tester cannot objectively verify it. A well-written NFR must be Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-sensitive. Example rewrite: 'A new user shall complete checkout in under 4 minutes without assistance 95% of the time.'

questions.q: The heating system story (a system that met all stated requirements but was too loud for a training room) illustrates which key principle about NFRs?
o: Technical specifications always override user comfort.
Users have unstated, implicit quality expectations that must be actively elicited during requirements gathering.
Noise is a functional requirement, not an NFR.
Requirements engineers should only document what users explicitly state.
questions.e: The heating story perfectly demonstrates that users have implicit quality expectations they don't think to mention. The BA's job is to surface these unstated needs through proactive elicitation - asking about all quality dimensions, not just functionality.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a nonfunctional requirement?
o: The system shall process payments within 2 seconds.
Only open source software under the GNU GPL may be used.
The user shall be able to purchase tickets online.
The system shall be available 99% of weekday hours.
questions.e: "The user shall be able to purchase tickets online" is a FUNCTIONAL requirement - it describes WHAT the system does. The others are NFRs: option A is a performance attribute, option B is a constraint, and option D is an availability attribute.

questions.q: Which quality attribute is classified as INTERNAL (important to developers, not directly visible to users)?
questions.e: Scalability-is-an-internal-quality-attribute- - -it-concerns-how-the-system-grows-to-handle-more-load,-which-is-mainly-a-developer/architect-concern.-External-attributes-(visible-to-users)-include-Availability,-Security,-Robustness,-Performance,-Reliability,-Safety,-Usability,-Integrity,-Interoperability,-and-Installability.

questions.q: An airport check-in kiosk is used infrequently by travelers who are strangers to the interface, and it handles payment transactions. Which pair of quality attributes should be prioritized HIGHEST for this system?
questions.e: The textbook uses this exact airport kiosk example. Usability is critical because most users encounter it infrequently and need to operate it without training. Security is critical because it handles payments. This is Step 2 of the quality attribute exploration method - reducing the list based on project context.

questions.q: Security is sometimes considered a subset of Integrity because some security requirements are intended to prevent unauthorized access to data.
questions.e: TRUE- - -The-textbook-explicitly-states-this.-Both-integrity-and-security-aim-to-protect-data:-integrity-prevents-data-loss/corruption-(from-any-source),-while-security-specifically-prevents-unauthorized-human-access.-Since-unauthorized-access-can-lead-to-data-corruption-or-loss,-security-falls-within-integrity's scope.

questions.q: From the Riyadh Seasons case study - which of the following is a NON-FUNCTIONAL requirement? (Past Exam - Major 1)
o: The customer shall be able to self-check in at the terminal using their ticket.
Upon self-check-in, the system shall issue the customer a bracelet with an electronic chip.
The online payment service shall complete transactions securely with no unauthorized access.
The system shall allow customers to load money onto their bracelets.
questions.e: Option C is a Security quality attribute (NFR) - it describes HOW WELL the system performs (securely), not WHAT it does. Options A, B, and D are all functional requirements - they describe specific behaviors and actions the system must perform.

questions.q: "Reliability is a lagging indicator." What does this mean?
o: Reliability requirements are always added late in the project.
You cannot determine whether a system has achieved its reliability requirements until it has been in operation for a period of time.
Reliability is less important than other quality attributes.
Reliability requirements lag behind performance requirements in priority.
questions.e: Reliability measures the probability of executing without failure over time. Unlike performance (which you can test immediately), you can't verify reliability until the system has been running in the real world for enough time to observe failure rates. This is why reliability requirements like MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) are measured retrospectively.

questions.q: Which requirement example best demonstrates the quality attribute of ROBUSTNESS?
o: The system shall be available at least 99% of weekdays between 8 AM and 6 PM.
If the text editor fails before the user saves, it shall recover the file contents from at most one minute prior to the failure.
No more than 5 experimental runs out of 1,000 can be lost due to software failures.
The system shall lock a user account after 3 failed login attempts within 5 minutes.
questions.e: Option B is the textbook's own example for ROBUSTNESS - it's about graceful recovery from an unexpected failure. Option A is Availability. Option C is Reliability (MTBF-related). Option D is Security. Robustness = how well the system handles and recovers from unexpected conditions.

questions.q: What is the key difference between Availability and Reliability?
o: They are the same quality attribute with different names.
Availability measures uptime percentage (accounts for repair time), while Reliability measures the probability of not failing over a period.
Reliability measures uptime percentage, while Availability is about graceful recovery.
Availability is an internal attribute; Reliability is external.
questions.e: Availability-=-MTBF-/-(MTBF-+-MTTR)- - -the-percentage-of-time-the-system-is-operational,-which-accounts-for-how-quickly-it-recovers.-Reliability-=-probability-of-NOT-failing-over-a-given-time-period.-A-system-can-be-reliable-(fails-rarely)-but-have-low-availability-(takes-very-long-to-restart-after-a-failure).

questions.q: Specifying "100% availability" is a valid, best-practice quality requirement for mission-critical systems.
questions.e: FALSE - The textbook explicitly warns against this. 100% availability is impossible to achieve and extremely expensive to pursue. Even "five 9s" (99.999%) - only 5 minutes 15 seconds of downtime per year - contributed to 25% of one system's total costs and virtually doubled hardware costs. Always specify realistic availability windows with maintenance exceptions.

questions.q: Which performance dimension does this requirement address? "At least 98% of the time, the trading system shall update the transaction status display within 1 second after the completion of each trade."
questions.e: This requirement specifies RESPONSE TIME (update within 1 second) with a probability constraint (at least 98% of the time). It's not throughput (transactions per second), not data capacity (records stored), and not dynamic capacity (concurrent users).

questions.q: Which requirement below is correctly written and verifiable? (Past Exam - Quiz 2 Style)
o: The system should be as fast as possible.
The system shall be secure and handle all failures gracefully.
A trained user shall submit a chemical request in an average of 3 minutes, and a maximum of 5 minutes 95% of the time.
The app must be user-friendly and available whenever needed.
questions.e: Option C is the textbook's own example of a well-written usability requirement. It passes SMART: Specific (chemical request), Measurable (3 min avg, 5 min max), Attainable, Relevant, Time-specific (95% of the time). Options A and D have vague/unverifiable terms. Option B combines two requirements using 'and' (a writing pitfall) and contains 'all failures' (wishful thinking).

questions.q: Why should you avoid the phrase "if possible" in a requirement, such as "Corporate project charge numbers should be validated online, if possible"?
o: It creates an escape clause - developers may skip the requirement, and it doesn't specify what to do when validation isn't possible.
questions.e: "If possible" is an escape clause - it makes the requirement optional and unverifiable. The textbook explicitly identifies this as a 'writing pitfall to avoid.' When you're unsure if something can be delivered, use TBD (To Be Determined) instead. The requirement also fails to specify what to do when the condition (validation unavailable) occurs.

questions.q: A stakeholder says: "The search results must appear in a dropdown list." As a BA, what should you recognize about this statement?
o: This is a clear functional requirement and should be documented as-is.
This may be a solution idea embedded as a requirement - the BA should identify the underlying need and document the dropdown as a design constraint if truly required.
This is an external interface requirement.
questions.e: The textbook warns that users often present 'requirements' that are actually solution ideas containing an embedded design constraint. The BA's job is to detect this - ask WHY they need dropdown results, understand the underlying search need, and then document the functional requirement with the dropdown as a constraint (only if truly necessary).

questions.q: Which of the following is a CONSTRAINT rather than a quality attribute requirement?
o: The system shall be available 99.5% of scheduled hours.
The application must use Microsoft .NET framework 4.5.
The system shall recover file contents from within 1 minute of an unexpected failure.
95% of new users shall complete registration without assistance.
questions.e: "The application must use Microsoft .NET framework 4.5"-is-an-architecture/implementation-constraint- - -it-restricts-the-developer's design choices without describing a user-observable quality. Options A and C are quality attribute requirements (availability and robustness). Option D is a usability requirement.

questions.q: Increasing security always has a positive effect on system performance.
questions.e: FALSE - Security and performance often conflict. Adding security layers (encryption, multi-factor auth, audit logging, access control checks) introduces overhead and latency, which can degrade performance. This is a classic trade-off. If security is prioritized higher than performance in your quality attribute matrix, you accept the performance penalty.

questions.q: Explain the five-step method for exploring quality attributes in a requirements engineering process. (Past Exam - Final Exam Style, 3pts)
questions.m:
Step 1 - Start with a broad taxonomy: Review all possible quality attributes to avoid overlooking any important dimension.
Step 2 - Reduce the list with stakeholders: Work with a cross-section of stakeholders to identify which attributes matter most for this specific project context.
Step 3 - Prioritize the attributes: Use pairwise ranking ('If I could have only one, which would I take?'). This also tells you how to resolve conflicts between attributes.
Step 4 - Elicit specific expectations: Ask targeted, domain-specific questions. Guide users through scenarios - they can't answer 'What are your reliability requirements?' but can answer scenario-based questions.
Step 5 - Specify using SMART: Write well-structured, Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-sensitive requirements. Avoid vague terms like 'user-friendly' or '24×7 available.'
questions.e: The 5-step method ensures quality attributes are systematically identified, prioritized, and correctly specified. Most requirements failures happen because steps 1-4 are skipped and engineers jump straight to writing vague quality statements.

questions.q: Distinguish between Reliability and Robustness as quality attributes. Why is Reliability called a 'lagging indicator'? Provide one concrete example requirement for each. (Past Exam - Midterm Style, 3pts)
questions.m:
Reliability: The probability of the software executing without failure for a specific period. Measures how rarely the system fails.
Example: 'No more than 5 experimental runs out of 1,000 can be lost because of software failures.'
Robustness: The degree to which a system continues to function properly when confronted with invalid inputs, hardware defects, attacks, or unexpected conditions. It's about graceful recovery.
Example: 'If the text editor fails before the user saves, it shall recover the file contents from at most one minute prior to the failure.'
Reliability is a 'lagging indicator' because you cannot verify it until the system has been operating in the real world for enough time to observe actual failure rates - unlike performance which can be tested immediately.
questions.e: Key distinction: Reliability = doesn't fail often. Robustness = handles failure gracefully when it does happen. A fragile system can be reliable until it meets one edge case, then crashes catastrophically. A robust system fails 'softly' and recovers.

questions.q: What problems do requirements engineers face when collecting and specifying quality requirements? Name at least three. (Past Exam - Major 1, 2pts)
questions.m:
1. Lack of domain expertise: Requirements engineers may not have the specialized knowledge needed to evaluate certain quality expectations precisely (e.g., understanding what 'reliable' means in a medical device).
2.-Implicit/unstated-expectations:-Users-often-have-quality-expectations-they-don't mention because they seem 'obvious' - like the noise in the heating system story. The BA must proactively elicit these.
3. Difficulty making requirements verifiable and measurable: Vague terms like 'user-friendly', 'fast', or 'secure' are hard to convert into objectively testable requirements.
4. Conflicting quality attributes: Improving one attribute (e.g., security) can degrade another (e.g., performance). Trade-off decisions require stakeholder negotiation.
5. Reliability as a lagging indicator: Some quality attributes (like reliability) can't be verified until the system has been in real operation - making upfront specification feel uncertain.
questions.e: The textbook discusses general problems with the requirements process, and quality requirements compound these because they are harder to specify precisely than functional requirements.
